meta.title: What a Brand Is: Equity & Assets

slides.title: What a Brand Is: Equity & Assets
slides.subtitle: A logo is the cheapest part of a brand. The expensive part lives in someone else's head.

slides.title: Kraft paid about £11.5 billion for Cadbury
slides.lead: Most of the reporting focused on the drama — the hostile bid, the factory promises, the political backlash. There is a quieter number buried in that 2010 deal.
slides.why: the chapter states one magnitude and refuses the rest — 'A large fraction of that price was for something that doesn't exist anywhere you can point to. Not factories. Not cocoa contracts. Not machinery.' It never puts a figure on the goodwill

slides.title: Two chemically identical bottles
slides.lead: The most direct way I know to see whether a brand is real: take acetaminophen, put one in a branded bottle and one in a generic, price them differently, and watch.
slides.why: the chapter runs a shared-origin experiment that separates at a named moment — identical chemistry, one label difference, and 'a measurable fraction of buyers pay more for the branded one. Every time. Across categories.'

data.splitLabel: one of them carries a name

tracks.label: the branded bottle
notes: signals what the experience will be

slides.title: An asset is something that produces future value
slides.lead: The delta in what buyers are willing to pay is brand equity made visible. It exists as surely as a machine that produces widgets, and it produces cash flows just as reliably.
bullets: **Price premium** — they pay more for the same thing.
**Retention** — they come back without being re-acquired.
**Forgiveness** — they give you the benefit of the doubt when something goes wrong.
None of that happens from a logo. It happens because of accumulated expectations living in specific people's minds. *Everything else is instrumental to that.*

slides.title: Awareness is the floor, not the goal
slides.lead: Keller's pyramid is worth understanding not as a taxonomy but as a *theory of accumulation*. Most of this book is, in one form or another, about this climb.
slides.why: the chapter reads the pyramid as an ordered climb — 'Salience is necessary. It is also, crucially, not sufficient… Resonance is rare. It cannot be bought directly. It is the output of doing every level below it well'

rungs.label: Salience
rungs.note: does the brand surface at the moment of decision?

rungs.label: Performance · Imagery
rungs.note: what it does · what it means socially

rungs.label: Resonance
rungs.note: customers seek you out, and recruit others

slides.title: Commodity on one side, fraud on the other
slides.lead: Every brand on the planet is trying to buy salience through advertising, and most of them stall there.
bullets: You need **both** sides of the second level: performance without imagery is a **commodity**; imagery without performance is a **fraud**.

The third level is where brand work starts to feel qualitatively different — explicit evaluations (*is this quality? do I trust this company?*) and the emotional responses the brand reliably triggers.
These are built slowly and degraded quickly. **A product recall wipes out years of quality judgment in a news cycle.**
Resonance is where the compounding asset actually lives — the tattoo, the installed base, the community.

slides.title: Keller gives you the shape. Aaker gives you the levers.
slides.lead: Aaker decomposes equity into four dimensions you can actually pull on.
bullets: **Awareness** — the salience layer, quantified. Unaided recall beats aided recognition; top-of-mind is the most valuable kind, because it governs habitual purchase.
**Perceived quality** — regularly diverges from objective quality. It is a *brand* effect, not a product effect. The perceived quality of a wine tracks its price label more than its chemistry.
**Associations** — the richest and most defensible dimension. The brand name is the activation trigger; **the network is the asset.** Fractured brands have contradictory nodes that cancel.
**Loyalty** — behavioral *and* attitudinal. A customer locked in by switching costs is not loyal; they leave the moment the cost drops.

slides.title: Find the weakest dimension. Intervene there.
slides.lead: Map your brand on all four dimensions. Intervening on a strong dimension produces little; intervening on the weak one produces the most lift.
bullets: This is not a market failure — it is how quality signals actually work when information is costly. **The brand is doing real work: reducing the buyer's estimation cost.**

When I talk later about positioning, what I mean at the cognitive level is building a particular association network in your target customers' minds — *before a competitor builds an incompatible one.*
Aaker's model stops at loyalty. **Brand evangelism** — when loyal customers actively recruit others — goes beyond this framework, and lands in **Chapter 12** as the output of a successful launch.

slides.title: Identity is what you project. Image is what lands.
slides.lead: These get used interchangeably in most business conversation. They are not interchangeable, and the confusion produces actual strategic errors.
bullets: **Brand identity** — the intended meaning, the strategy made visible. The ad, the spokesperson, the packaging, the price point. *The sender's side.*
**Brand image** — the associations actually perceived by the receiver. It is empirically measurable: ask enough customers and you have it.

**Brand equity** — the *value* generated when the image is favorable and the gap between identity and image is small. Not a message. Not a perception. **The downstream consequence of managing that gap.**

slides.title: The gap is where equity leaks
slides.lead: Brand work, when it is working, is the management of the distance between identity and image. Two named leaks, and one you have to go find.
slides.why: the chapter names a membrane and two specific crossings that fail — 'When a company says "premium" and customers experience "overpriced," that's a gap — equity is leaking. When a company projects "innovative" and customers encode "unreliable," that's a gap with a different leak.'

inside.label: what the last recall taught them

slides.title: Kapferer's prism forces you to say it out loud
slides.lead: A useful diagnostic on the identity side: six facets mapped as a hexagon, so nothing stays vague.
bullets: Sender side — **physique**, **personality**, **culture**.
Receiver side — **self-image**, **reflection**, **relationship**.
The image-side counterpart is qualitative research. The equity measurement is what comes next.
The point of the prism is not the hexagon. It is that a facet you cannot articulate is a facet you are not managing.

slides.title: Three firms, three anchors, one arbitration standard
slides.lead: The valuations differ substantially across methods for the same brand. That is not a bug to be embarrassed about — **brand valuation is a model, not a measurement.** The chapter itself tags these methods for re-verification, so this grid grades only what it states.
slides.why: the chapter compares Interbrand, Kantar BrandZ and Brand Finance on what each anchors its method in, notes ISO 10668 as the standard 'all three firms reference', and carries an explicit [verify] tag on the methodology specifics

slides.title: Machine gathers. Human judges.
slides.lead: The equity audit has two layers that should not be collapsed. The failure mode is letting the output of the first layer do the work of the second.
slides.why: the chapter sorts the audit into exactly two named buckets and says so as its takeaway — 'the pattern that repeats across every AI-assisted brand task: machine gathers, human judges'

data.note: Sentiment is not equity. A brand can be positive at salience and have no resonance — and Harley-Davidson's owners complain about quality and still tattoo the logo on their arms.

slides.title: Pass · Fail · Cannot-determine — with evidence
slides.lead: Five criteria on the audit you produce. Every verdict is yours, and none of them exists until you run it.
slides.why: the chapter's validation exercise lists five ordered criteria and instructs 'Rate each criterion Pass / Fail / Cannot-determine with evidence' — the verdicts depend entirely on the reader's own run

gates.label: Failure-mode
gates.rule: no sentiment score passed off as a verdict

output.label: an equity read you can defend

slides.title: Cite no valuation figure unless you can source it.
slides.lead: Run the baseline on your own brand: awareness signals, associations clustered into themes, a sentiment read, a competitor contrast. Tag every claim you cannot tie to a source [UNVERIFIED] — and leave the equity level blank. That column is yours. You now know what your equity *is*; next comes who it is *for*, because equity is built in specific minds, not in general.
